GAGA theorem

Words: 55
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
For a projective variety over the complex numbers, analytification gives an equivalence between algebraic and analytic coherent sheaves, preserves their cohomology, and is fully faithful on their morphisms. In particular, a holomorphic isomorphism between algebraic line bundles is algebraic. This allows a complex-torus proof of a line-bundle identity to establish the corresponding algebraic identity on a projective elliptic curve.

Very general point of an algebraic parameter space

Words: 50
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
A property holds at a very general point of an irreducible complex algebraic parameter space if it holds outside a countable union of proper Zariski-closed subsets. This permits countably many exceptional conditions. Over C that complement is nonempty and dense, for example by the Baire category theorem on a local smooth analytic chart.

Hilbert scheme (HilbP(X))

Words: 513 Articles: 8
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
For a projective scheme X and a fixed Hilbert polynomial P, the Hilbert scheme parametrizes flat families of closed subschemes of X with that polynomial. This turns a family of embedded algebraic curves into an algebraic parameter space.

Hilbert functor (HilbX/k​)

Words: 203 Articles: 2
Hilbert scheme OurBigBook.com
For a projective scheme X over a field k, the Hilbert functor assigns to a k-scheme T the set of closed subschemes W⊆X×k​T which are of finite presentation, proper and flat over T. Pullback of families makes it a contravariant functor. After choosing a very ample line bundle, requiring a fixed fibre Hilbert polynomial P gives the subfunctor represented by HilbP(X). The unrestricted functor is represented by the disjoint union of these Hilbert schemes.

First-order embedded deformation

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Hilbert functor OurBigBook.com
A first-order embedded deformation of a closed subscheme Z⊆X is a closed subscheme Zε​⊆X×k​Spec(k[ε]/(ε2)) flat over the dual numbers and with special fibre equal to the given embedded Z. It is a tangent vector of the Hilbert scheme, not a deformation modulo arbitrary automorphisms of the ambient scheme. These deformations are naturally the global sections of the normal sheaf.
Zariski tangent space of a Hilbert scheme (T[Z]​Hilb(X)=H0(Z,NZ/X​))
Words: 77
First-order embedded deformation OurBigBook.com
For a closed subscheme Z⊆X with ideal sheaf I, one has T[Z]​Hilb(X)≅HomOX​​(I,i∗​OZ​)≅H0(Z,NZ/X​). Locally a flat deformation ideal J⊆A[ε]/(ε2) satisfies J∩εA=εI. Lifting f∈I to f+εg∈J gives a well-defined map f↦gmodI killing I2. Conversely the graph condition gmodI=ϕ(f) defines an ideal with flat quotient by the flatness criterion over dual numbers. These operations commute with restriction and are inverse, giving the global identification without a smoothness assumption.

Fano scheme (Fk​(X))

Words: 275 Articles: 4
Hilbert scheme OurBigBook.com
The closed subscheme of the Grassmannian parametrizing projective k-planes contained in an embedded projective variety X.

Fano scheme of lines (F1​(X))

Words: 258 Articles: 3
Fano scheme OurBigBook.com
The Fano scheme for projective lines. For X⊆P3, it is a closed subscheme of Gr(2,4) and hence is projective. Requiring the defining homogeneous polynomials of X to vanish along a line gives its closed defining conditions.
Incidence proof that a cubic surface contains a line
Words: 159 Articles: 1
Fano scheme of lines OurBigBook.com
Cubic forms in four variables form P19. Lines form the four-dimensional Grassmannian G=Gr(2,4). The incidence pairs (ℓ,[F]) with F∣ℓ​=0 form a projective-space bundle with fibre P15 over G, since restriction to a line imposes four independent linear conditions. Hence the incidence variety is irreducible of dimension 19. For F=x02​x2​+x12​x3​, a nearby line written x2​=a0​x0​+a1​x1​, x3​=b0​x0​+b1​x1​ lies on F precisely when all four parameters vanish. This is an isolated point of that fibre. The fiber dimension theorem forces the image to have dimension 19, and projectivity makes the image closed. It is therefore all of P19, proving geometric existence over an algebraically closed field.
Cubic surface line incidence variety (I={(L,[F]):F∣L​=0},dimI=19)
Words: 53
Incidence proof that a cubic surface contains a line OurBigBook.com
A projective bundle with fibre P15 over the four-dimensional Grassmannian Gr(2,4). The condition of containing a fixed line imposes four independent linear conditions on the twenty cubic coefficients. The projection to P19 is proper. The line {x2​=x3​=0} is an isolated point over x02​x2​+x12​x3​; isolated fibre point forces dominance in equal dimensions then proves that every cubic surface contains a line.
Finiteness of lines on a smooth surface of degree at least three
Words: 63
Fano scheme of lines OurBigBook.com
For a line L on a degree-d smooth surface in P3, the adjunction formula gives L2=2−d. If d≥3, all lines are negative curves, hence there are only countably many by countability of negative curves. Their projective Fano scheme of lines cannot have a positive-dimensional complex component, since such a component has uncountably many points. A zero-dimensional projective scheme of finite type has finitely many points, proving the assertion.

Étale cohomology (Heti​(X,F))

Words: 58
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
Étale cohomology is sheaf cohomology on the site whose objects are étale morphisms Y→X and whose coverings are jointly surjective families of such morphisms. It provides cohomological invariants for algebraic varieties over fields of positive characteristic. In Deligne-Lusztig theory, compactly supported groups with ℓ-adic coefficients, for ℓ different from the field characteristic, give finite-dimensional representations of the finite groups acting on the varieties.

Algebraic set (V(I))

Words: 51
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
An algebraic set is a zero locus of polynomial equations, allowing reducible sets. An affine algebraic set uses ordinary polynomial equations; a projective algebraic set uses homogeneous equations in projective coordinates. On affine or projective space, closed sets in the Zariski topology are algebraic sets, and an irreducible algebraic set is an algebraic variety in the classical convention.

Complex multiplication

Words: 216 Articles: 3
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
An abelian variety of dimension g has complex multiplication when its rational endomorphism ring contains a commutative semisimple Q-algebra of dimension 2g. For an elliptic curve in characteristic zero, this means its geometric endomorphism ring of an elliptic curve is an order in an imaginary quadratic field. The resulting rank-one Tate module representations connect torsion points to class field theory.

CM period (Ω∞​,Ωp​)

Words: 58
Complex multiplication OurBigBook.com
A complex CM period compares an algebraic invariant differential on a CM elliptic curve with its analytic lattice coordinate. At an ordinary prime, a p-adic CM period compares the same differential with the invariant differential of the multiplicative formal group: an isomorphism η is normalized by logE​η(T)=Ωp​log(1+T). Matched periods make normalized critical Hecke L-function values algebraic and give precise p-adic L-function interpolation.

CM reciprocity theorem

Words: 70
Complex multiplication OurBigBook.com
For a complex CM torus C/a and an idele s of its CM field, the automorphism corresponding to s by Artin reciprocity takes its lattice to s−1a and acts on torsion through the adelic scalar s−1. When the curve is defined over a larger field, use the idelic norm to the CM field. Comparison with the original curve gives a scalar in the CM field, producing the Hecke character of a CM elliptic curve.

CM elliptic curve

Words: 43
Complex multiplication OurBigBook.com
An elliptic curve with complex multiplication is called a CM elliptic curve. Distinguish geometric endomorphisms from endomorphisms defined over the base field. In characteristic zero, adjoining the imaginary quadratic field selected by the tangent action makes all geometric endomorphisms defined over the base. Good split primes have ordinary reduction; good inert primes have supersingular reduction.

Birational geometry

Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com

Blowing up (algebraic geometry, BlZ​X)

Words: 120 Articles: 2
Birational geometry OurBigBook.com
The projective morphism ProjX​⨁j≥0​Ij→X associated to the powers of the ideal sheaf of a closed centre. Off that centre it is an isomorphism. Blowing up a smooth point of an n-dimensional smooth variety replaces the point by a projective space Pn−1, the algebraic exceptional divisor.

Strict transform of an algebraic subvariety (Y=π−1(Y∖Z)​)

Words: 33
Blowing up (algebraic geometry) OurBigBook.com
For a blowup of an algebraic variety π:X→X with centre Z, the strict transform of an algebraic subvariety of a subvariety Y not contained in Z is the closure of π−1(Y∖Z). It excludes components supported entirely in the algebraic exceptional divisor.

Algebraic exceptional divisor (E)

Words: 43
Blowing up (algebraic geometry) OurBigBook.com
The divisor contracted by a blowup of an algebraic variety to its centre. For the blowup of a smooth point on an n-dimensional smooth variety it is Pn−1. Being a closed projective subvariety of positive dimension, it can obstruct affineness of a fibre containing it.

Zariski topology

Words: 98 Articles: 2
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
The Zariski topology on an affine scheme SpecA has closed sets V(I)={p:I⊆p} for ideals I⊆A. Its basic open sets are the principal open subschemes D(f).

Zariski cover

Words: 31
Zariski topology OurBigBook.com
A Zariski cover of a scheme is a family of open immersions whose images cover its underlying topological space. Such families define the Zariski topology as a Grothendieck topology on the category of schemes; a cover need not be finite.

Zariski dense subset

Words: 40
Zariski topology OurBigBook.com
A subset of an algebraic variety is Zariski dense when its closure in the Zariski topology is the whole variety. For an affine variety, this is equivalent to saying that every regular function vanishing on the subset vanishes on the entire variety.

Presheaf of sets on a topological space

Words: 919 Articles: 19
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
A presheaf of sets on a topological space X is a contravariant functor from the inclusion-ordered category O(X) of open subsets to Set. Its maps F(U)→F(V) for V⊆U are restriction maps.

Constant presheaf of sets (KT​(U)=T)

Words: 43
Presheaf of sets on a topological space OurBigBook.com
Every restriction is the identity. Its stalk at each point is T, and its étale space of a presheaf is X×T with T discrete. It is generally not a sheaf; in particular its value on the empty open set is T. Its sheafification is the constant sheaf of sets.

Morphism of presheaves (η:F→G)

Words: 23
Presheaf of sets on a topological space OurBigBook.com
A natural transformation between presheaves assigns maps F(U)→G(U) commuting with every restriction. For presheaves of abelian groups or modules, those maps preserve the specified algebraic structure.

Sheaf (mathematics)

Words: 820 Articles: 16
Presheaf of sets on a topological space OurBigBook.com
A sheaf of sets is a presheaf in which compatible sections on any open cover glue to one unique section on the union.
A sheaf may additionally carry abelian group or module structure on its sections, with restriction and gluing preserving that structure. The underlying sheaf of sets retains the same local-to-global axiom.

Skyscraper sheaf of sets (i∗​S(V)=S if x∈V,i∗​S(V)=1 otherwise)

Words: 41
Sheaf (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
For inclusion of a point i:{x}→X, this is the direct-image sheaf of a set. It is right adjoint to the stalk functor. It uses the singleton terminal set on opens omitting x, rather than the zero group used for abelian-group skyscraper sheaves.

Étale space of a presheaf (Et(P)=∐x∈X​Px​)

Words: 53
Sheaf (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
The space of germs of a presheaf has basic opens given by the germs of one section over an open set. Projection to its base point is a local homeomorphism. The sections are locally constant functions into a discrete set T, with ordinary restriction. It is the sheafification of the constant presheaf of sets. Its value on an empty open set is a singleton, even if T is empty. For a topological space, this construction is left adjoint to the global sections functor: a map from it to a sheaf is a family of global sections indexed by T.

A linear system of divisors is a projective family of effective Weil divisors linearly equivalent to a fixed divisor. A complete linear system of a divisor contains every effective representative of that class; a projective subspace gives a subsystem. For a Cartier divisor, the family is obtained from global sections of its associated line bundle. The algebraic curve case recovers the usual moving family of effective divisors.

Irreducibility is a separate assertion and requires suitable hypotheses on the associated morphism; a pencil composed with a map to a curve can have disconnected general divisors.

On a smooth projective curve of genus two, D=K+P+Q has three sections and no base points by the Riemann-Roch theorem. Its map to P2 is nondegenerate and has mapping degree times image degree four. The only nonbirational possibility is a double cover of a conic. Every degree-two divisor with two sections is canonical, again by Riemann-Roch theorem, so that possibility forces D∼2K, or P+Q∼K. If this equivalence fails, the image is a quartic and the map is birational. The quartic is singular because a smooth plane quartic has genus three.

A nonempty closed subset which, with its induced topology, is an irreducible topological space. In an affine algebraic set these subsets correspond, with reversed inclusion, to prime ideals of the coordinate ring.

In any topological space, the closure C of a point x is an irreducible closed subset. If C=A∪B with A,B closed in C, then both are closed subsets of the ambient topological space. One contains x, so it contains all of C by the definition of closure. Equivalently, x is a generic point of C. This does not assert that every irreducible closed subset of an arbitrary topological space has a generic point.

This is the supremum of lengths of strict chains of nonempty irreducible closed subsets. Closedness is relative to the given space. This is the relevant dimension for locally closed subsets of algebraic varieties, rather than a general Hausdorff-space notion of dimension.

The supremum of the lengths of strict chains of nonempty irreducible closed subsets. It is the maximum of the dimensions of the irreducible components. Residual intersection through a curve pencil (λP+μQ=RS)

Bézout's theorem OurBigBook.com
Suppose two degree-n projective plane curves meet at n2 distinct points, and nm of them lie on an irreducible degree-m curve R=0, with m<n. Pick an extra point of R=0 outside the finite base locus. A nonzero linear combination H=λP+μQ vanishes at that point. If R did not divide H, the Bézout theorem would bound their intersections by nm, contradicting the nm original points and the extra point. Therefore H=RS with degS=n−m. All remaining base points lie off R=0 and hence on S=0. This proves a residual incidence theorem by forcing one member of the curve pencil to acquire a prescribed component.

Bézout's theorem OurBigBook.com
For projective plane curves without a common irreducible component, project from a point outside both curves. In coordinates where that point is [1:0:0], their defining homogeneous polynomials have constant nonzero leading coefficients in X. The resultant in X is nonzero by Gauss's lemma, and is homogeneous of degree degCdegD in the remaining two coordinates. Every intersection projects to one of its zeros. Each projection line has only finitely many intersections with the curves, so their intersection is finite. Choose the center again outside all joining lines of pairs of intersection points; the projection is now injective on that finite set, proving the bound.

Cayley-Bacharach theorem OurBigBook.com
Let two triples of projective lines meet in nine distinct points. Any plane cubic containing eight contains all nine. To prove this, write the triples as F=L1​L2​L3​ and G=M1​M2​M3​, with the missing point on L3​. The candidate cubic H agrees with a scalar multiple of G on L1​, so H−λG=L1​Q. Its three known zeros on L2​ force Q=L2​L. Two remaining known zeros on L3​ force the linear factor L to be a multiple of L3​. Hence H=λG+μF and vanishes at the missing point.

For two smooth plane conics meeting transversely, the operation of crossing a chord of the second conic tangent to the first and choosing the other tangent through the new endpoint acts as a translation on an elliptic curve on their incidence curve. Maximum number of flexes of a smooth plane curve (3d(d−2))
Words: 155
Inflection point of an algebraic plane curve OurBigBook.com
A nonsingular complex projective plane curve of degree d≥2, with no common irreducible component with its Hessian curve, has at most 3d(d−2) distinct flexes. The Hessian criterion for a flex identifies the flexes with the intersection, and Bézout's theorem counts its total intersection multiplicity. Higher contact can make this bound on distinct points strict.
For a general nonsingular curve of degree d≥3, all flexes have tangent contact exactly three, making the bound an equality. For a fixed point and line through it, contact at least four imposes four independent linear conditions on the coefficients; the space of such point-line pairs has dimension three. Thus degree-d equations with contact at least four form a proper closed exceptional locus. In local graph coordinates y=h(x), the Hessian determinant along the curve is a nonvanishing factor times h′′(x), so contact exactly three makes the intersection simple. A nonsingular plane conic has no flexes; a line is excluded because its tangent is a component and its Hessian determinant is identically zero.

On E×E for a complex elliptic curve, the two factor curves and the diagonal have intersection matrix ​011​101​110​​, of determinant two. Their cohomology classes are therefore independent. The cycle class map thus shows that the diagonal is outside that image, proving failure of surjectivity.

Chern class axioms in the Chow ring (ci​(E)∈CHi(X))

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Chern class OurBigBook.com
For a vector bundle E of rank r on a smooth algebraic variety, algebraic Chern classes have c0​(E)=1, vanish for i>r, commute with pullback, and obey the Whitney sum formula for Chern classes for every short exact sequence of vector bundles. A line bundle O(D) has total class 1+[D]. The projective-bundle splitting construction makes pullback injective and supplies a filtration by line bundles, so these axioms determine all classes as elementary symmetric functions of their first classes. In particular, ci​(E∗)=(−1)ici​(E) and c1​(L⊗M)=c1​(L)+c1​(M) in the ordinary Chow ring.

Chern class in complex cobordism (cjMU​(E)∈MU2j(X))

Words: 124 Articles: 1
Chern class OurBigBook.com
The complex orientation of complex cobordism defines Chern classes of actual complex bundles by the splitting principle and elementary symmetric expressions in the first Chern classes of line summands. For an actual rank-n complex bundle, its top Chern class is its Euler class in a generalized cohomology theory. Chern classes extend stably by the Whitney formula; this stable extension must not be confused with the Euler class of a merely stably complex real bundle.

Chern number (⟨ci1​​⋯cis​​,[M]⟩)

Words: 53
Chern class OurBigBook.com
On a compact oriented 2r-manifold without boundary, an integral product of Chern classes of total complex degree r pairs with the fundamental class to give a Chern number. A unitary connection supplies Chern-Weil theory representatives, but the integer is independent of that connection. The Second Chern number on a four-manifold is one important example; the integral of the First Chern class over a closed surface is another.

For a rank-r complex vector bundle, let h=c1​(S∗) for the tautological line S on its projective bundle. The Leray-Hirsch theorem gives the free basis 1,h,…,hr−1 over base cohomology. The uniquely determined coefficients in the displayed monic relation define the integral Chern classes. The line normalization uses the Euler class of the canonically oriented underlying real two-plane bundle, and uniqueness makes this definition intrinsic and natural under pullback. No choice of a trivializing cover or classifying map remains in the definition.

Euler sequence OurBigBook.com
For a degree-zero rational function regular on an open subset of projective space, each derivative ∂f/∂Xi​ is a regular homogeneous rational function of degree −1. These derivatives define a derivation with values in O(−1)⊕(n+1), hence a map from the Kähler differential sheaf. The last map is (gi​)↦∑i​Xi​gi​. On Xi​=0, put yj​=Xj​/Xi​ and use frame Xi−1​. The derivative of yj​ has coordinate vector with 1 at j, −yj​ at i and zero elsewhere. Those vectors form a free basis of the kernel of (bi​)↦bi​+∑j=i​yj​bj​, proving exactness directly in every characteristic.

Near a projective subspace, transverse directions are linear maps from the tautological line to the complementary coordinate vector space. This describes the actual complex normal bundle. The conjugate line and the dual line are complex-isomorphic using a Hermitian metric; neither is the original tautological line as a complex bundle in general.

For an oriented closed surface smoothly embedded in an oriented four-manifold, a transverse section of the normal bundle gives a homologous small push-off. A framing of an embedding Sk−1↪Nn−1 is a trivialization of its rank-(n−k) normal bundle, equivalently a continuously varying ordered basis of normal vectors. After fixing one framing, homotopy classes of orientation-compatible framings form a torsor for [Sk−1,SO(n−k)].

Elimination theory

Words: 28
Algebraic geometry OurBigBook.com
Elimination theory studies how to remove variables from systems of polynomial equations. A resultant eliminates one variable from two equations; back-substitution and checks in the original equations recover and verify full solutions.
